                                       NOTICE OF APPEAL

        Physicians for Social Responsibility Iowa (PSR Iowa), Petitioner herein, by and through

counsel and pursuant to 10 C.F.R. § 2.311(c), hereby gives notice of its appeal to the U.S.

Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC or Commission) from the Atomic Safety and Licensing

Board’s (ASLB) ruling, LBP-26-9, “Memorandum and Order (Denying Request for Hearing)”

(September 24, 2026)1 (ASLB Decision) in this proceeding.

        PSR Iowa appeals from and seeks reversal of the ASLB’s underlying determinations and

the Board’s overall decision which denied admission of Petitioner’s proffered Contentions 3 and

5 and asks for adjudication.

                                                        /s/ Wallace L. Taylor
                                                        Wallace L. Taylor, Esq.

                                                        /s/ Terry J. Lodge
                                                        Terry J. Lodge, Esq.
                                                        Co-Counsel for Physicians for Social
                                                        Responsibility Iowa

                               BRIEF IN SUPPORT OF APPEAL

                                         INTRODUCTION

        In 2024, NextEra Energy Duane Arnold LLC (NextEra) filed with the NRC several

license amendment requests (LARs) in support of NexEra’s plan to return the permanently shut

down Duane Arnold Energy Center (Duane Arnold) to power operations. As a shutdown plant,

Duane Arnold had been placed in decommissioning status.

        Both NextEra and NRC staff have admitted that “NRC regulations do not prescribe a

specific regulatory path for reinstating operational authority.” 2 NextEra is relying for restart on a

1
  Memorandum and Order (Denying Request for Hearing), NextEra Energy Duane Arnold, LLC (Duane
Arnold Energy Center). Docket No. 50-331-LA, LBP-26-9 (September 24, 2026) (ADAMS No.
ML26267A223) (ASLB Decision).
2
 r NextEra letter to NRC, Regulatory Path to Potential Reauthorization of Power Operations at the Duane
Arnold Energy Center, January 23, 2025 (ML25023A265).


                                                                                                         5
 scheme cobbled together by Holtec Decommissioning International 3, with the complicity of the

NRC,4 to attempt to use existing regulations to restore the operating license of the Palisades

Nuclear Plant in Michigan. This plan includes a proposed exemption from the certifications

provided pursuant to 10 C.F.R. § 50.82 for permanent shutdown and removal of fuel from the

reactor, and for an LAR to revise the license and technical specifications to support resumption

of power operations at Palisades.

        The Petitioner, Physicians for Social Responsibility Iowa (PSR Iowa), timely filed a

Petition to Intervene And Request for Adjudicatory Hearing 5 on June 22, 2026, pursuant to a

notice in the Federal Register. The Petitioners included five proposed contentions of law and fact

in their Petition. NextEra and the NRC Staff timely answered the Petition, and the Petitioners

replied in support of the Petition. Oral argument directed at contention admissibility took place

on August 13, 2026.

        On September 24, 2026, the assigned ASLB issued a ruling that granted legal standing to

PSR but denied all of its contentions to be inadmissible for hearing. Contention 1 explained that

the purpose and need statement in the Environmental Assessment (EA) issued by the NRC stated

that the purpose and need was to restart Duane Arnold, thus eliminating any other alternative.

Contention 2 explained that the discussion of alternatives in the EA was limited to restarting

Duane Arnold and the no action alternative, thus avoiding a discussion of alternative sources of

power, especially renewable energy sources. Contention 3 asserted that there was no regulatory

 pathway to restarting Duane Arnold and that the exemption request and LARs submitted by

NextEra were not a valid application of the existing regulations. Contention 4 pointed out that the

EA does not adequately discuss and evaluate the impact of climate change on Duane Arnold and

the impact of Duane Arnold on climate change. Finally, Contention 5 asserted that the ER

improperly segments the restart of Duane Arnold from the impact of the Google data centers to

which Duane Arnold is committed to providing power.

       PSR is appealing only Contentions 3 and 5 for review by the Commission.

    ARGUMENT: THE ASLB ERRED IN REJECTING PETITIONERS’ CONTENTIONS

                                         CONTENTION 3

       PSR presented its Contention 3 as follows:

       NextEra admits that there is no provision in law or regulation for the NRC to authorize
       the restart of Duane Arnold as a closed reactor. NextEra is cobbling together a “pathway”
       to restart, using a “creative” procedure based on existing regulations that it believes
       allows NextEra to simply reverse the decommissioning process established by 10 C.F.R.
       § 50.82. Since there is no dedicated regulatory procedure for restarting a closed reactor,
       the NRC has no authority to approve the license amendments requested by NextEra.

       The ASLB determined, and PSR agreed, that Commission precedent in the Commission’s

decision on this identical issue regarding the attempted restart of the Palisades Nuclear Plant 6

prevented a decision finding that Contention 3 is admissible.7 To be clear, however, PSR objects

to the ASLB’s ruling and continues to assert that Contention 3 is admissible for the reasons stated

in PSR’s Petition to Intervene and Request for Adjudicatory Hearing.

       PSR Iowa stated for the record at the oral argument to determine admissibility of

contentions,8 and the ASLB acknowledged,9 that PSR is pursuing Contention 3 in order to


6
  Holtec Decommissioning International, LLC and Holtec Palisades, LLC (Palisades Nuclear Plant),
CLl-26-7, 103 NRC __, __ (slip op. at 22).
7
  ASLB Decision p. 6.
8
  Oral Argument Transcript, pp. 25-26 (August 13, 2026) (ML   ).
9
  Id., p. 60.


                                                                                                    7
 preserve the issue presented by Contention 3 for judicial review. PSR also notes that the

Palisades decision is on judicial review to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of

Columbia Circuit.10 In support of its argument in this appeal and to preserve the issue for judicial

review, PSR relies on the facts and arguments asserted at pp. 25-31 in its Petition to Intervene

And Request for Adjudicatory Hearing and incorporates the same by reference as though

published herein.

          Based on the foregoing, PSR requests that the Commission either reverse the ASLB or

render a decision on Contention 3 that preserves the issue for judicial review.

                                        CONTENTION 5

          In Contention 5, PSR Iowa asserted that NextEra has improperly segmented the proposed

project for purposes of investigating and compiling an environmental document to comply with

NEPA. PSR Iowa argued that the proposed project includes the Duane Arnold Energy Center and

induced development in the form of the planned Google data center complex to be constructed in

or geographically proximate to Palo, Iowa within three miles from Duane Arnold. By limiting the

scope of the project for NEPA purposes solely to the DAEC, PSR Iowa maintains that NextEra

has not addressed prospective cumulative climate change impacts caused by these interrelated

projects, heat island effects caused by the geographic proximity of the two facilities extending

miles outward from each and that there would be combined impacts from high-volume water

usage for cooling both facilities with water drawn from the Cedar River.

          The Atomic Safety and Licensing Board agreed that PSR Iowa had “put forth sufficient

facts to establish a basis for the geographic and temporal proximity of the data center to DAEC,

which would be built near the facility and roughly contemporaneously with the DAEC restart.” 11


10
     D.C. Circuit Case No. 26-1221.
11
     ASLB Decision p. 31.


                                                                                                     8
 The Board acknowledged that PSR Iowa had “adequately” pled (1) that Google (or an affiliated

company) intends to build a data center close to DAEC; (2) that the data center, perhaps in

combination with another data center in Cedar Rapids, will use nearly all of the planned

electrical generation of DAEC; (3) that NextEra has signed a contract in which Google has

agreed to purchase the power for a period of 25 years; and (4) that the two projects will proceed

closely in time.12

          The Board, however, found Contention 5 to be inadmissible for five stated reasons. 13 As

demonstrated below, the Board misinterpreted the Supreme Court’s interpretation of the National

Environmental Policy Act in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, 145 S. Ct.

1497, 1517 (2025) (Seven County), and seems to believe that NEPA confers the authority to veto

a project – which it doesn’t – and denied the petition in part based on that misunderstanding.

          PSR Iowa serially rebuts the Board’s five conclusions below.

                A. ‘But for’ causal relationship” between two projects “is insufficient
                         to make an agency responsible for a particular effect”

          The ASLB asserts the precept from Seven County that “a ‘but for’ causal relationship

between two projects ‘is insufficient to make an agency responsible for a particular effort’”

should provide an adequate rationale for refusing to consider the Duane Arnold resumption of

operations cumulatively with the nearby Google data center to be constructed within three miles

of Duane Arnold. It does not suffice. NEPA still forbids segmentation here.

          Justice Kavanaugh in Seven County further stated, “NEPA calls for the agency to focus on

the environmental effects of the project itself, not on the potential environmental effects of future

or geographically separate projects. A relatively modest infrastructure project should not be



12
     Id. at fn. 128.
13
     ASLB Decision pp. 31-33.


                                                                                                     9
 turned into a scapegoat for everything that ensues from upstream oil drilling to downstream

refinery emissions.”14

          The NRC’s conundrum is that it cannot claim the data center is a future, geographically

separate action when the Duane Arnold restart is contractually and economically connected,

geographically proximate, and contemporaneous undertaking, and the restart is impossible

without it. Since Google’s data centers (a large one within a couple of miles and a smaller one in

Cedar Rapids, 10 miles away) are the exclusive customer, Duane Arnold and the facilities form a

single, functionally integrated project that must be evaluated under a single, unified

environmental review. The Duane Arnold restart’s environmental implications and

spatial-economic relationship to Google fall within, not outside, Seven County’s broad “but for”

caveat.

              B. The Petitioner has not asserted that the proposed data center combined
                            with the DAEC restart is a single federal project

          It’s true that PSR Iowa does not contend that the Google data center and Duane Arnold

are a single federal project, but it is unnecessary from a segmentation standpoint that they be so.

          The involvement of a NEPA-regulated federal project with a nonfederal project has the

effect of “federalizing” the overall action for NEPA purposes. Impermissible segmentation in a

major federal action occurs where part of that action has been “segmented" in order to escape

application of the NEPA process. Save Barton Creek Ass’n v. Federal Highway Admin., 950 F.2d

1129, 1140 (5th Cir. 1992). The hallmark of improper segmentation is the existence of two

proposed actions where the proposed component action has little or no independent utility and its

completion may force the larger or related project to go forward notwithstanding the

environmental consequences. Maryland Conservation Council v. Gilcrest, 808 F.2d 1039, 1042


14
     Seven County, 605 U.S. 190.


                                                                                                    10
 (4th Cir. 1986); Bragg v. Robertson, 54 F. Supp.2d 635, 649 (S.D. W.Va. 1999). Segmentation of

a project to avoid federal jurisdiction is unlawful. Historic Pres. Guild of Bay View v. Burnley,

896 F.2d 985, 986 (6th Cir. 1989) (per curiam).

        The crucial issue is whether the various actions, when combined, have an effect on the

environment that might be overlooked if examined separately. That is certainly the circumstance

here. Both nuclear reactors and massive data centers release staggering amounts of waste heat

and have intense water-cooling demands. By arbitrarily ruling that the Google data center project

need not be considered within the NEPA investigation for the restart of Duane Arnold, the NRC

ignored the possible effects of thermal pollution in the shared watershed and microclimate heat

islands.15 Those effects are inevitable regardless of the NRC’s pretense that location of a massive

heat-generating data center functionally adjacent to a massive heat-generating nuclear reactor

doesn’t portend express changes to the environment.

        Agencies must not be permitted to segment an obviously integrated relationship so as to

disguise their environmental effects. See Taxpayers Watchdog, Inc. v. Stanley, 819 F.2d 294, 298

(D.C.Cir. 1987) (“The rule against segmentation was developed to insure that interrelated

projects the overall effect of which is environmentally significant, not be fractionalized into

smaller, less significant actions”). Multiple stages of a development must be analyzed together

when “[t]he dependency is such that it would be irrational, or at least unwise, to undertake the

first phase if subsequent phases were not also undertaken.” Thomas v. Peterson, 753 F.2d 754,

759 (9th Cir. 1985). A federal agency may not segment a project under NEPA where approval of

the segment under consideration will result in any irreversible or irretrievable commitments to


15
  At p. 38 of the Petition for Leave to Intervene, PSR Iowa alleged that “NextEra has committed to
construction of entirely new mechanical draft cooling towers at DAEC,68 but has performed no analysis
of the changes in efficacy and evaporation rate in light of global warming nor of the possible implications
for changing local humidity and precipitation events.


                                                                                                         11
 remaining segments of the proposed action. United States Dep’t of Energy et al. (Clinch River

Breeder Reactor Plant), CLI-82-23, 16 NRC 412, 424 (1982). Multiple projects must be

considered together where they are contemporaneous, connected, closely related, and

interdependent. Delaware Riverkeeper Network v. FERC, 753 F.3d 1304, 1317 (D.C. Cir. 2014).16

An overweening purpose of NEPA is to stop an agency from impermissibly segmenting

“connected . . . federal actions into separate projects and thereby fail[ing] to address the true

scope and impact of the activities that should be under consideration.” Id. at 1313. Although the

Google data center is not itself a “federal” project, it nonetheless is inextricably intertwined with

the Duane Arnold reopening and is federalized for purposes of NEPA.

        Moreover, “projects have substantial independent utility for purposes of the connected-

action inquiry only when both projects are independently useful.” City of Port Isabel v. FERC,

111 F.4th 1198, 1213 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (emphasis added). Port Isabel considered two proposed

natural gas export terminal projects which were to be constructed on the Brownsville Shipping

Channel in Texas. One company sought permission from the Federal Energy Regulatory

Commission (FERC) to build a liquified natural gas (LNG) export terminal there, and

contemporaneously, a pipeline company filed an application to FERC to construct and operate a

new interstate pipeline system to deliver natural gas from existing grid interconnects in Nueces

County, Texas, to the LNG terminal. Together, the two actions formed a single project. The

project was challenged under several federal laws including NEPA. After a remand from the D.C.


16
  “The upgrade projects were completed in the same general time frame, and FERC was aware of the
interconnectedness of the projects as it conducted its environmental review of the Northeast Project. The
end result is a new pipeline that functions as a unified whole thanks to the four interdependent upgrades.
         FERC has not shown that there are logical terminii between the new segments of the Eastern Leg
or that each project resulted in a segment that has substantial independent utility apart from the other parts
of the Eastern Leg. Rather, FERC merely argues that one terminus was “no more logical than another,”
Br. of Resp’t at 25, and that the capacity added by each project was contracted separately. These
explanations are insufficient to address Riverkeeper’s segmentation claim.”


                                                                                                           12
 Circuit Court, the LNG terminal filed a proposal on a separate docket to add a carbon capture and

sequestration (CCS) system to its design to remove carbon dioxide emissions during natural gas

liquefaction and transport those emissions by pipeline to an underground injection well for

sequestration.

       The D.C. Circuit explicitly ruled that FERC committed a legal error by failing to treat the

CCS system as a “connected action” under NEPA. The court rejected the idea that they could be

severed for environmental review purposes simply because the LNG facility could technically

operate without it, noting that the CCS system had a clear functional nexus to the overall project

design. For the projects to escape joint review, both must have substantial independent utility.

While the terminal could technically run without carbon capture, the carbon capture facility had

absolutely zero purpose or capability to exist without the terminal.

       Hence the NRC must prove that both the Duane Arnold restart and the Google data center

projects are independently useful, but it can’t. Reopening an economically non-competitive,

shutdown nuclear plant lacks independent economic utility without a dedicated tech hyperscale

buyer to subsidize it. Duane Arnold has no economic viability unless there is a premium paid by

a tech hyperscaler.

       To separate the restart from the data center would be “arbitrary and capricious” under the

Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The nuclear plant and the data center are interdependent

parts of a larger action that depend on each other for their justification.

                 C. “The NRC would have no ability to mitigate or otherwise alter
                           the environmental effects of the data center”

       The ASLB strains to show that the Google data center has independent utility, claiming

that “the NRC could deny every LAR at issue but that would not prohibit Google from

proceeding to build and operate its data center if it could obtain the necessary electrical power


                                                                                                    13
 from another source.” ASLB Decision p. 32. Sheer speculation as to possibilities is not factual;

there is no showing that this particular suggestion has any basis in reality.

       The ASLB somehow failed to understand that mitigation or alteration of the

environmental effects of the data center is not a primary objective of NEPA. The “twin aims” of

NEPA are, rather, to obligate an agency to consider every significant aspect of environmental

impact, and to “ensure[ ] that the agency will inform the public that it has indeed considered

environmental concerns in its decisionmaking process.” Baltimore Gas & Electric Co. v. Natural

Resources Defense Council, Inc., 462 U.S. 87 (1983). NEPA's public disclosure requirements

ensure that relevant environmental information is made available to the larger public audience so

they can participate in the agency's decision-making process. Weinberger v. Catholic Action of

Hawaii/Peace Education Project, 454 U.S. 139 (1981).

       No one – certainly not PSR Iowa – claims that the NRC has the power to mitigate

projects over which it has no legal control. The agency does, however, have the obligation to

factually articulate the environmental effects arising from analysis of the nuclear power plant’s

resumed operations and the Google data centers as a unified project, which might provide a basis

for mitigation of the project over which the NRC has control (such as cooling towers).

   D. The Board’s allegation that the NRC should disapprove DAEC license amendments
      because of disapproval of a DAEC customer
       Surprisingly, the ASLB accuses PSR Iowa of assuming that NEPA noncompliance allows

a project to be vetoed: “[T]to the extent that Petitioner suggests the NRC should disapprove the

DAEC license amendment, not because there is a problem with the plant, but because the NRC

disapproved of a DAEC customer, this is problematic.” ASLB Decision p. 32. PSR Iowa

suggests that there is NEPA noncompliance because of segmentation of two clearly-connected

actions that must be analyzed as a single, unified project.



                                                                                                    14
           PSR Iowa seeks to have the NRC to discharge its responsibility to consider every

significant aspect of environmental impact, and to ensure that it will inform the public that it has

indeed considered environmental concerns in its decisionmaking process. The Board’s suggestion

that PSR Iowa believes there is a NEPA veto available to stop the Duane Arnold restart is either a

non sequitur or a red herring.

      E. NEPA analysis required because of PSR Iowa’s showing that the environmental
         effects of constructing the planned data center would be useful to the NRC’s
         decision on whether to approve the LARs at issue

          The ASLB determined that, “Absent Petitioners putting at issue that studying the

environmental effects of constructing the planned data center would be useful to the NRC’s

decision on whether to approve the LARs at issue, which it did not, NEPA does not require such

a study.” The Board claimed that NEPA’s “rule of reason” shielded the NRC from having to

undertake a more intense analysis.17 While after Seven County, as Justice Sotomayor put it,

“NEPA requires consideration of environmental impacts only if such consideration would result

in information on which the agency could act,” PSR Iowa had no obligation to provide a detailed

mitigation plan to have Contention 5 admitted. The ASLB superimposed additional admissibility

requirements on a contention that was already adequately asserted.

          The NRC’s contention admissibility standards require petitioners to “proffer at least some

minimal factual and legal foundation in support of their contentions.” Duke Energy Corp.

(Oconee Nuclear Station, Units 1, 2, and 3), 49 NRC 328, 334 (1999). This was done by PSR

Iowa in pointing out the geographic proximity of Duane Arnold and a planned large Google data

center within three miles of the nuclear power plant, along with some scientific citations

asseverating that there would be heat island problems and pointing out the combined demands


17
     Board Decision p. 32.


                                                                                                  15
 for water for the power plant and data center as part of the cumulative effects that should be

investigated under NEPA. The pleading requirements of 10 C.F.R. § 2.309(f)(1) do not

encompass the ASLB’s burdensome expectation that PSR Iowa was required to show “that

studying the environmental effects of constructing the planned data center would be useful to the

NRC’s decision on whether to approve the LARs at issue.” In sum, the ASLB applied 10 C.F.R.

§ 2.309(f) as a “fortress to deny intervention,” prohibited by Duke Energy Corp., supra at 335.

Contentions need only have “some reasonably specific factual or legal basis.” Entergy

NuclearVermont Yankee, LLC, and Entergy Nuclear Operations, Inc. (Vermont Yankee Nuclear

PowerStation), 82 NRC 211, 221 (2015) (internal quotation marks omitted).

        NEPA’s text commands federal agencies to utilize a systematic, interdisciplinary approach

to ensure that “presently unquantified environmental amenities and values may be given

appropriate consideration in decisionmaking.” 42 U.S.C. § 4332(B). PSR Iowa asserted

materiality of Contention 5 to the proposed restart by pleading that “the NRC must consider

reasonably foreseeable impacts of the proposed project on climate change” 18 and that there must

be “consideration of climate change vulnerability and resilience impacts under NEPA upon the

proposed project.”19 In Contention 5, PSR Iowa stated in part:

        The entire project must be evaluated for purposes of identification and consideration of
        alternatives and mitigation steps. The true nature of the project must be revealed in order
        to accurately understand the regional environmental impacts on the physical environment
        of east central Iowa and the health and well-being of its residents.

        Notwithstanding the strictures imposed on NEPA by Seven County, NEPA continues to

require agencies to take a "hard look" at environmental consequences. Calvert Cliffs'

Coordinating Committee, Inc. v. U.S. Atomic Energy Commission, 449 F.2d 1109 (D.C. Cir.


18
   Petition for Leave to Intervene and Request for Adjudicatory Hearing, p. 42,
https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML2617/ML26173A206.pdf
19
   Id. p. 43.


                                                                                                  16
 1971). An agency cannot effectively evaluate the significance of an action's impacts in total

isolation. Forcing an agency to blind itself to adjacent or concurrent projects would allow major

environmental degradation to occur via a “death by a thousand cuts” where unconsidered but

related projects combine to create a catastrophic localized or regional impact. Ignoring this

reality violates NEPA’s explicit statutory goal to “attain the widest range of beneficial uses of the

environment without degradation.”20

                                          CONCLUSION

          The pleading requirements of 10 C.F.R. § 2.309(f)(1) do not encompass the overly

burdensome standards that were repeatedly applied by the ASLB against the PSR Iowa. The

standards are not meant to be used as a “fortress to deny intervention,” Duke Energy Corp.

(Oconee Nuclear Station, Units 1, 2, and 3), 49 NRC 328, 335 (1999). Yet here, once again, they

were. PSR Iowa provided the requisite “reasonably specific factual or legal basis.” Entergy

Nuclear Vermont Yankee, LLC, and Entergy Nuclear Operations, Inc. (Vermont Yankee Nuclear

Power Station), 82 NRC 211, 221 (2015) (internal quotation marks omitted). The Petitioner

“proffer[ed] at least some minimal factual and legal foundation in support of their contentions.”

Duke Energy Corp.supra at 334. But it was unavailing. Consequently, PSR Iowa now looks to

the Commission to review the matters they have raised in this Brief, reverse the Atomic Safety

and Licensing Board, and remand Contentions 3 and 5 to the ASLB for adjudication on the

merits.
